title: Optimal private sample complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization
formal: Editorial zero-order variant: determine the sample complexity of uniformly polynomial-time central \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-private algorithms returning \(X\in\mathbb R^d\) with \[\mathbb E\,\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_\alpha F(X))\le\beta\] for all population objectives in the normalized class below. Determine matching upper and lower bounds up to factors polynomial in \(\log(2+d+1/\alpha+1/\beta+1/\varepsilon+1/\delta)\). Expectation includes the independent dataset and algorithm randomness.
definitions:
The decision variable is \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), with Euclidean norm. Each component obeys \(|f(x;\xi)-f(y;\xi)|\le L\|x-y\|_2\) for all x,y. Assume the expectation defining F is finite and an initial point \(x_0\) is given with \(F(x_0)-\inf_x F(x)\le\Phi\). No convexity or differentiability is assumed. The dataset consists of N independent samples from P; the empirical loss is their average, a different objective from F.

For a locally Lipschitz function h, its Clarke subdifferential \(\partial h(x)\) is the closed convex hull of limits of gradients at differentiability points approaching x. For \(\alpha>0\), define the Goldstein subdifferential \(\partial_\alpha h(x)=\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{\|y-x\|_2\le\alpha}\partial h(y)\). A point is \((\alpha,\beta)\)-Goldstein stationary when \(\inf_{g\in\partial_\alpha h(x)}\|g\|_2\le\beta\). The radius alpha and residual beta are separate parameters. This does not assert local or global minimality.

Datasets are adjacent when one sample is replaced. Approximate central privacy means that for every adjacent D,D' and measurable output event E, \(\Pr[A(D)\in E]\le e^\varepsilon\Pr[A(D')\in E]+\delta\). Privacy must hold on all datasets, while utility is measured on independent samples from the population. The private output is the returned point; raw sample-dependent oracle evaluations are internal. The source analyzes function-value oracles and also discusses gradient access, and distinguishes single-pass from multiple-pass methods.

For this selected variant set \(L=\Phi=1\), \(x_0=0\), \(d\ge1\), \(0<\alpha,\beta,\varepsilon\le1/2\), and \(0<\delta\le\varepsilon/100\). Components are jointly measurable in the sample and location, globally 1-Lipschitz, with finite population expectations. The input consists of N independently sampled component-function oracles. A zero-order call supplies a sample index i and a real vector x and returns the exact value f(x;xi); gradients and subgradients are not available. Calls may be adaptive and samples may be reused. Each call costs one operation, in addition to the cost of constructing its d-dimensional argument. Use an exact-real RAM with arithmetic +, −, ×, ÷, square roots and comparisons, and independent uniform real draws in [0,1], each charged one operation. All sampled and returned quantities must be measurable. There is no uncharged optimization or integration oracle. One uniform algorithm family must have expected total operation count bounded by one fixed polynomial in N, d, 1/alpha, 1/beta, 1/epsilon, and log(1/delta), on every dataset in the component class. It must terminate almost surely. Privacy holds on every pair of adjacent datasets in that class, not only typical samples. The utility requirement is expected population Goldstein residual, not a per-sample or empirical condition. These access, cost, normalization, parameter and utility choices are editorial specifications of the source’s broader question.
answer_criterion: Give a sample bound \(U(d,\alpha,\beta,\varepsilon,\delta)\), a single uniform algorithm attaining it under the stated cost bound, and a lower bound \(L\) against every algorithm obeying the same model, with \(U/L\) bounded by a fixed polynomial in the displayed logarithm throughout the parameter domain. Prove privacy, expected population utility, sample and time bounds in Lean. Lower bounds for a larger algorithm class are admissible; bounds restricted to a smaller oracle class are not. State any computational assumption explicitly; conditional lower bounds yield only a conditional characterization. An algorithm for component-wise relaxed stationarity does not meet this target.
context:
Kornowski, Liu and Talwar improve sample requirements for private nonsmooth nonconvex optimization using Goldstein stationarity. They separate one-pass population methods from empirical optimization followed by a generalization result.

Their discussion explicitly calls for tight lower bounds. The appendix gives evidence involving computationally inefficient methods and a relaxed stationarity definition; that result is not an efficient solution of the target here.
why: The tradeoff connects privacy, statistical sample size and a general notion of stationarity beyond smooth optimization.

import_provenance.original_title: Optimal private sample complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization
import_provenance.original_statement: Determine the optimal sample complexity for polynomial-time (ε,δ)-private algorithms finding approximate Goldstein-stationary points of Lipschitz, nonsmooth, nonconvex population losses with bounded initial suboptimality. The target is a tight dependence on dimension, privacy, neighborhood radius and stationarity error, closing the upper/lower-bound gap in Talwar’s joint 2025 work.

sentences: The data define a nonsmooth, nonconvex population objective.
A private algorithm must return a point whose nearby generalized gradients have a small convex combination.
The target concerns sample efficiency under a polynomial computation requirement.
The source improves upper bounds and separates population, empirical and relaxed stationarity guarantees.
The editorial variant fixes zero-order access, expected population residual, uniform polynomial computation and matching sample bounds up to polylogarithmic factors.
